{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"b62cf2c90af7dcf4d1064b2cee0a6ca89574b1777784c6f23222ae06ca973ea2","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:15","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Occupant protection and vehicle condition confusables","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: primary versus secondary belt rules, child seat thresholds, air bag switches, brake types, carbon monoxide and mirrors","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: primary versus secondary belt rules, child seat thresholds, air bag switches, brake types, carbon monoxide and mirrors
Confusable pairs among seat belt, child seat, air bag and vehicle-condition rules, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec04-R01 | anchor: A01
An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under 18 can be the only reason for a traffic stop, whereas an unbelted back-seat rider aged 18 or older can be ticketed only after a stop for something else. [A01]
Why it matters: group seat belts; confusable primary versus secondary enforcement.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-R02 | anchor: A01
An ordinary driver answers for belting passengers under 18, but a GDL permit or probationary license holder must make passengers of every age buckle up. [A01]
Why it matters: group seat belts; confusable ordinary versus GDL driver duty.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-R03 | anchor: A01
A driver who carries a passenger using a wheelchair must secure that person with a correctly adjusted, fastened wheelchair and occupant securement device. [A01]
Why it matters: group seat belts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-R04 | anchor: A01
Survival odds in a crash are three to four times better when a motorist wears both a seat belt and a shoulder strap. [A01]
Why it matters: group seat belts; confusable sixty percent versus three to four times.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-R05 | anchor: A01
Buckling up takes only about three seconds. [A01]
Why it matters: group seat belts; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-R06 | anchor: A02
Belts slow the body down together with the vehicle and keep occupants from being thrown out in a crash, so injuries are likely to be less severe. [A02]
Why it matters: group seat belts; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-R07 | anchor: A02
Never fasten one belt around two people. [A02]
Why it matters: group seat belts; misconception sharing a belt.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-R08 | anchor: A03
Three child-seat thresholds are easy to mix up: under age two or under 30 pounds means rear-facing, under four and under 40 pounds means a harness in a rear seat, and under eight and under 57 inches means a harness or booster in a rear seat. [A03]
Why it matters: group child passengers; confusable age and weight thresholds.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec04-R09 | anchor: A04
An autocycle operator may not carry any child who would have to ride in a child passenger restraint under the child passenger safety law. [A04]
Why it matters: group child passengers; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-R10 | anchor: A04
In 1995 NHTSA allowed air bag cutoff switches in pickup trucks, sports cars and cars with no back seat, and from January 1998 it let repair shops and dealers install switches after an approved application. [A04]
Why it matters: group air bags; difficulty high.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-R11 | anchor: A04
A switch for both driver and passenger air bags is for people whose medical condition makes a deploying air bag riskier than hitting the wheel, dashboard or windshield. [A04]
Why it matters: group air bags; difficulty high.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-R12 | anchor: A05
A driver-side air bag switch is for drivers who cannot keep at least 10 inches between the steering wheel center and the breastbone center, while a passenger-side switch is for drivers who must seat an infant, or a child aged 1 to 12, in front. [A05]
Why it matters: group air bags; confusable driver-side versus passenger-side switch.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec04-R13 | anchor: A05
An infant should always ride in a rear-facing infant safety seat in the back seat of a vehicle that has air bags. [A05]
Why it matters: group air bags; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec04-R14 | anchor: A05
Besides the steering wheel and dashboard markings, makers may place air bag warning labels on the sun visors, on the sides of the open-door frame, or in the owner's manual. [A05]
Why it matters: group air bags; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec04-R15 | anchor: A06
Conventional disc and drum brakes are pumped gently after driving through water, while anti-lock brakes are pressed steadily and never pumped. [A06]
Why it matters: group brakes; confusable conventional versus anti-lock.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-R16 | anchor: A06
On very soft surfaces such as loose gravel or unpacked snow, anti-lock brakes may make the stopping distance longer. [A06]
Why it matters: group brakes; misconception ABS always shortens stops.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-R17 | anchor: A06
Get a helper to check the brake lights, and replace broken light covers because their glare can affect the driver behind. [A06]
Why it matters: group lights; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-R18 | anchor: A07
High and low beams must both work and be aimed correctly; other drivers flashing their lights at your low beams may mean your headlights are out of line. [A07]
Why it matters: group lights; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-R19 | anchor: A07
On a straight, level road the vehicle should keep a straight course with no front-end shimmy and without excess play in the steering wheel. [A07]
Why it matters: group vehicle condition; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-R20 | anchor: A07
When the turn signals fail, repair them quickly and give hand signals until they work again. [A07]
Why it matters: group vehicle condition; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-R21 | anchor: A08
The snow and ice fine applies whether or not any snow or ice actually comes loose from the vehicle. [A08]
Why it matters: group snow and ice; misconception fine needs a falling chunk.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-R22 | anchor: A08
Driving with an exhaust leak or a poorly tuned engine, or with the trunk or rear tailgate open, can let carbon monoxide build up. [A08]
Why it matters: group carbon monoxide; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-R23 | anchor: A09
Carbon monoxide can also build up from holes in the vehicle body, from a tailpipe blocked by snow, leaves or water, and from idling in a garage or other enclosed space even with the outside door open. [A09]
Why it matters: group carbon monoxide; misconception open garage door.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec04-R24 | anchor: A10
To cut night glare, skip colored lenses because they distort color, and choose anti-reflective lens coatings. [A10]
Why it matters: group vision; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec04-R25 | anchor: A11
With age, visual clarity and side vision fade; in the manual's example, a person of 60 takes in only about one third of the light that a person of 20 does. [A11]
Why it matters: group vision; difficulty medium.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-R26 | anchor: A11
To check the mirrors on the road, let a car pass on the left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should already show in the outside mirror. [A11]
Why it matters: group mirrors; difficulty medium.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-R27 | anchor: A11
Some situations allow longer idling, such as sitting in traffic or waiting at a drive-thru, so the three-minute limit has listed exemptions. [A11]
Why it matters: group idling; confusable limit versus exemptions.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]
